turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mrs Khumalo? I'm Sister Jacobs. We'll do your readings before Doctor Naidoo calls you in. Have you been sitting quietly a few minutes?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Can we just get on with it? I'm tired, and that waiting room is freezing with the load shedding.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Shame. Left arm out, please. I'll be as quick as I can.

[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Blood pressure is one hundred and fifty two over ninety four. Pulse seventy six. Oxygen ninety eight percent. Temperature thirty six point four. And you're sixty eight kilograms, same as last time.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): The pressure's worse, I knew it. I haven't been sleeping either, but don't start lecturing me.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): I won't. Any allergies I should put on the file — tablets, food, anything?
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None.

[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): Afternoon, Mrs Khumalo. Sorry, I got held up just now. Sister's written one fifty two over ninety four, pulse seventy six. This visit is really a routine look at the blood pressure and the cholesterol. How are you, actually?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Tired. Irritable, if you ask them at work. My husband wants the garden done, the bakkie's at the mechanic, so ja. Wonderful week.
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Are you still taking both — the cholesterol tablet and the blood pressure one?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure one, yes. The cholesterol one, well, actually, I stopped that.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): The atorvastatin, your cholesterol tablet?

[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, the white one, one at night. I thought it was forty milligrams, but no, the box says twenty. I read this long article online about statins damaging your muscles and your memory, and I just stopped. I'm not—
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did you stop it?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I can't pin the date. Maybe six weeks, maybe two months, after I saw that article. I really don't know.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): All right. And the amlodipine, the blood pressure tablet, five milligrams — every day, as we agreed?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Every other day. I take one, I skip a day, I take one. I didn't want the pressure going too low.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to scold you. I just need what's true. Any chest pain?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Short of breath when you walk?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I walk to the robot and back every morning, that's fine. The pavement is a disgrace, but that's not your problem.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Muscle aches — calves, thighs, shoulders — anything?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Dizziness? Headaches?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No dizziness. Headaches, no. I'm fine.

[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me think out loud. We've been treating the high blood pressure and the high cholesterol. Pressure's up, the amlodipine is only every second day, statin stopped. Simplest thing is restart the atorvastatin tonight, twenty milligrams, and see you in two weeks to—
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not restarting it tonight. You can explain, but don't just put it back in my hand.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): —to see that you're tolerating it. Hear the reasoning, at least.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): My husband leaves his diabetes pills on the kitchen counter. Metformin, I think, the big ones, five hundred. I nearly took one on Tuesday, thought it was mine. I didn't, hey. Those are his.

[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good that you spotted it. His metformin does not go on your list. Coming back to you — you said no muscle pain. Is that the whole story? That article was all about muscles.

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Well... actually, both calves. A deep ache at night, not a proper cramp, worse when I've been standing. A few weeks now, and that's half of why I stopped, not only the internet.
[SEG0032] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry, Doctor, I'm interrupting — the lab sent March's result. Total cholesterol was 6.2.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): 6.2, only mildly up. Thank you, Sister. Mrs Khumalo, how many nights a week is that ache?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): The taxis were late this morning, that's why I was short with the desk. Sorry, Sister. Eish.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): The calves, maybe four nights a week, not every night. I wake at about three anyway, so I lie there and notice it. Sleep's been rubbish for ages.

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. That changes what I just said. I am not restarting the statin today, and two weeks is the wrong interval. Bloods first — a lipid panel, liver tests, and a CK, the muscle enzyme — and we look at those before any statin decision.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not two weeks. A month. We'll revisit the statin decision in a month, here, with the results.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): A month, if the roster allows. The shifts are...
[SEG0039] person_1 (NURSE): I can book those bloods downstairs for this afternoon. Lipids, liver, CK.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ja, please, today. That's the list.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Headaches. You said no. I'm asking once more, because a pressure like this can give you a sore head.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I said no.

[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): It's been pounding, though — I shouldn't have said no. Afternoons, behind both eyes, about three times this week. When it started I can't tell you, a while, and I just get cross when everything gets blamed on the pressure.
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Pounding, behind the eyes, afternoons. Any spots, flashing lights, blurred vision with it?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): No spots, no blurring. It eases if I lie down in a dark room. Coffee does nothing, I already tried.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): My first instinct was to send you for a CT of the head today. New headaches, pressure up.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): A scan? The medical aid will drag their feet, and I don't even know if they'll—

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm changing that — no scan today. They're not sudden, your eyes are fine, and half the amlodipine has been missed. If the headaches do not settle once you're on the blood pressure tablet every day, we might do a scan, not before.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): So every day. Not every other day.
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Five milligrams, every morning, every day. Not your husband's pills. If you feel faint, or properly dizzy, phone the rooms — don't quietly skip a dose.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Every morning. I'll try. I forget things when I'm this washed out. Don't give me that look.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): This tiredness — is it new, or has it been months?
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Months, and it was there before I stopped the cholesterol tablet. I'm finished by lunch. My daughter says I'm irritable, and she's not wrong, I just hate hearing it.
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever? Weight up or down? Feeling cold in yourself?
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. Weight's the same, Sister just said. I feel cold in the evenings, but the house is cold, so I don't think that's me.
[SEG0056] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor, should I add a glucose? She mentioned diabetes tablets.

[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): Those are the husband's, not hers. A fasting glucose did cross my mind while we're taking blood, but no, don't add it — lipids, liver enzymes, CK. We might add a glucose later if something else comes up, but not today.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't have sugar. He does. Please don't mix the two of us up. I've said it.
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't. Family history — strokes, heart attacks, high cholesterol in the family?
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had a stroke, around seventy. My dad drank, but no stroke that I know of. I live with my husband, the house in Kensington, if you need that.
[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mother, a stroke. Noted. Do you smoke?
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): I stopped. Three years ago. It was about ten a day before that. And wine — a glass some weekends, not more.
[SEG0063] person_3 (DOCTOR): Exercise, besides that walk to the robot?
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): That's it. Mornings. I'm not a gym person.
[SEG0065] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Appendix out, when I was twenty-something. Don't ask the year, it's gone.
[SEG0067] person_3 (DOCTOR): Appendix only. Let me look at those calves.
[SEG0068] person_3 (DOCTOR): Both calves are soft, there's no swelling and no redness, and the foot pulses are present. Nothing on examination that looks like a clot.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): So it's not an emergency. Can we finish? I want the bloods and then I want the couch.

[SEG0070] person_3 (DOCTOR): Nearly. Working impression, not a final label: I think the headaches are probably from the blood pressure sitting high while the amlodipine's been every other day. The calf ache I'm leaving open — could be the statin from before, could just be the standing. We're not deciding that today.

[SEG0071] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the plan, one version: bloods this afternoon, lipid panel, liver tests, and CK, and no glucose. Amlodipine five milligrams every single morning, and do not restart the atorvastatin yourself. We see you in a month to revisit the statin decision. If the headaches have not settled by then, we might arrange the head scan.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): And if the calves get worse before the month is up?

[SEG0073] person_3 (DOCTOR): If they're worse before then, or you get chest pain, sudden weakness, or a headache that's the worst you've ever had, come in sooner or go to casualty. Otherwise the month stands.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. A month. I'll take the tablet in the mornings. I'm still tired and I'm still cross, so don't expect smiles in the passage.
[SEG0075] person_1 (NURSE): I'll walk you to the lab. Form says lipids, liver, CK — no glucose.
[SEG0076] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Sister. We'll see you in a month, Mrs Khumalo.

spec.situation: Patient on routine review who admits stopping the cholesterol tablet after reading something online, still takes the BP tablet but 'every other day'; mentions husband's diabetes pills; doctor does not scold, plans repeat blood tests and revisits the statin decision in a month.
features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

bad.reason: All details supported except certainty; patient states headache clearly, not uncertain.
bad.text: headache (category=neurological, status=present, severity=pounding, frequency=about three times this week, mostly in the afternoons, temporality=current, body_site=behind both eyes, relieving_factors=lying down in a dark room, reported_by=patient, certainty=uncertain)

bad.reason: Total cholesterol completed is supported, but it was sent by lab, not requested by nurse.

Negative finding omitted: no blurred vision with the headaches.

Symptom/history detail omitted: patient feels cold in the evenings, though she attributes it to the house being cold.
History omitted: no known stroke history in her father.

There was a real change/disagreement about statin management: doctor first proposed restarting atorvastatin 20 mg that night and review in 2 weeks, patient objected, and after calf-pain history the doctor changed plan to not restart it and review in 1 month after blood tests.

omissions.text: Atorvastatin was stopped by the patient because of concern from an online article about statins harming muscles and memory, and she initially refused the doctor's suggestion to restart it that night.

The patient denied muscle aches initially, but later clarified she does have bilateral deep calf aching at night; this contradiction/changed history is not captured as a disagreement in the interaction.
The patient denied headaches initially, then corrected herself and reported pounding headaches; this flipped negation/change in symptom history is not captured as such.
Negative finding missing: no muscle aches was specifically asked and initially denied before the patient later revised the history.
Negative finding missing: no headaches was specifically asked and answered twice before the patient revised the history.
Headache detail missing: headaches ease if she lies down in a dark room.

Negative finding recorded wrongly: 'headache relief with coffee absent' is inaccurate; the patient said coffee does nothing, which is not a denied symptom/findings category but a lack of benefit from coffee.
Sleep disturbance detail missing: she wakes at about 3 a.m. anyway, which is part of her poor sleep history.
History detail missing: the tiredness had been present before she stopped the cholesterol tablet.
Family history detail missing: father drank alcohol heavily, though no stroke was known.

Assessment/plan change missing: the doctor first considered restarting atorvastatin tonight and seeing her in two weeks, but changed plan after learning about calf pain—no statin restart now, blood tests first, and follow-up changed from two weeks to one month.

Investigation consideration and reversal missing: the doctor said his first instinct was to send her for a CT head that day because of new headaches and high blood pressure, then decided against scanning that day.
Negative finding missing from examination/assessment: doctor stated nothing on calf examination looked like a clot.
